summary: Tobermory's wooden light of 1885: keepers who farmed out the work, a keeper who vanished in 1895, and an automated light since 1952.

lens.note: fourth-order apparatus from 1929, replacing a seventh-order lens (LighthouseFriends)

structures.type: hexagonal wooden tower with iron lantern

access.note: Grounds open and a parking area at the end of Big Tub Road; tower closed to visitors.

facts.agency: Canadian Coast Guard (owner); Municipality of Northern Bruce Peninsula (site manager, per the Lighthouse Directory)

events.note: Wooden tower built for $675 by John George and David Currie of Port Elgin on the point where Charles Earl had hung his lantern
Fixed red dioptric light, 40 ft above the lake, visible 8 miles (1885 departmental description, as LighthouseFriends prints it)
Wooden frame keeper's dwelling erected near the light (year to 30 June 1905)
Hand fog horn given to Keeper Currie for signals from nearby vessels; the 1912 report lists a hand fog horn at Tobermory
Pathway and viewing area built; LighthouseFriends credits Friends of Fathom Five, the Lighthouse Directory Friends of Bruce District Parks
Powerful winter storm washed away part of the foundation and some shingles; repaired
Recognized federal heritage building (Lighthouse Directory gives 1992; LighthouseFriends says early 1990s)
Tobermory residents petition the federal government for ownership under the Heritage Lighthouse Preservation Act; outcome not found in the sources read
Some damage in a storm in November 2019; repairs under way in summer 2020

keepers.name: Charles Earl
keepers.note: Hung a lantern on a tree at night from 1881; paid $100 a year by departmental letter for keeping a light; in temporary charge when Davis was appointed

keepers.name: Abraham Davis
keepers.note: First appointed keeper of the 1885 tower; disappeared in November 1895 after leaving in a skiff for the wrecks of the Owen Sound and Worts

keepers.name: Henry Bradley Davis
keepers.note: Son of Abraham Davis; appointed over his mother Flora Davis; dismissed in 1901

keepers.name: Henry Martin
keepers.note: Named 'Henry Marten' in Davis's 1898 letter. Employed by the keeper to attend the light (Harty's 1901 report, as LighthouseFriends prints it); not a departmental appointment

keepers.name: Daniel Butchart
keepers.note: Hired after Davis was dismissed; sacked in 1903 when the light was suffering for want of a keeper

keepers.name: Archibald Currie
keepers.note: Salary $250 from 1903; listed at Tobermory in the 1904 report's index of lightkeepers; a 1907 letter said he slept at his farm; given a hand fog horn in 1910

keepers.name: John Henry Smith
keepers.note: Baptist fisherman from St. Catharines; present at the station at the 1914 inspection; resigned in 1926, aged eighty

keepers.name: Thomas Andrew Hopkins
keepers.note: Veteran of the First World War; the last keeper; the light was electrified and automated in 1952

wrecks.outcome: Keeper Abraham Davis left for the scene in a small skiff and was not seen again
wrecks.note: The report does not say where the vessels lay beyond the keeper's errand

wrecks.outcome: Totally destroyed by fire at Tobermory harbour; cause unknown
wrecks.note: The report places the fire in the harbour; it does not link it to the light

wrecks.outcome: Grounded on Yeo Island in the vicinity of the Tobermory station; a party went ashore in a small boat; released 27 August and went on to Depot Harbour
wrecks.note: The report says 'Tobermory station' without saying whether it means this light

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The Commissioners recommended a light at Tobermory in 1857, but none was built; Charles Earl showed a lantern from 1881 under a departmental allowance. The first lighthouse tower and the departmental light date from 1885.

notes_for_editor: Sources: LighthouseFriends (copyrighted; facts paraphrased, one or two sentences quoted in evidence only) carries most of the keeper history, including the 1885 departmental description and a Kingston News item of November 1895 that LighthouseFriends quotes; the newspaper is cited as quoted by LighthouseFriends, not read. The 1885 and 1880s-1890s departmental reports are not in the local corpus (marine_ca starts with the report for the year to June 1900), so LighthouseFriends is the only source for them. Keepers Earl to Smith (1881-1926) are LighthouseFriends' list; the 1904 index is the only departmental line checked (Currie). Henry Martin is not a departmental keeper and has role 'other'. Disagreements: the tower height is 12.0 m in the station record (Wikidata) but 12.5 m in LighthouseFriends and the Lighthouse Directory, and the focal height is 13.2 m (LighthouseFriends and CCG) against 13 m (Wikipedia, not cited). The 1985 pathway is credited to Friends of Fathom Five (LighthouseFriends) and to Friends of Bruce District Parks (Lighthouse Directory). The heritage designation year is 1992 (Directory) or early 1990s (LighthouseFriends). The 2012 petition outcome was not found; the Directory says the Municipality of Northern Bruce Peninsula has applied for ownership and is site manager, so the owner may have changed since. The 1922 'Tobermory station' in the Marine report is not identified as this light. Canadian 1946-1991 keeper detail for this station is not in the corpus. The 1904 index cited for Archibald Currie is an alphabetical list of lightkeepers and stations in the corpus OCR; the Currie line was matched by position, so re-check the scan (p. 208) before publishing. The 1885 range is given as eight miles and is kept in the report's unit (no nautical conversion). FACT-CHECK 2026-10-27: every footnoted sentence was checked against the cached LighthouseFriends page, the Lighthouse Directory and the Canadian Register entry, and the corpus page of each Marine report (Currie index p.208, dwelling p.40, fog horn p.78, Alaska p.198, Kearsarge p.152 confirmed by the OCR page index). Changes to the story: the Kearsarge sentence had 'so' (no wireless, so a party went ashore); the source says 'but'. Davis's 1898 denial and resignation (in LighthouseFriends' quotation of his letters) were left out, so 'Davis was dismissed' in 1901 read as abrupt; now stated, with the Department's inaction until 1901. The endorsement that Flora Davis had performed the duties for five or six years is now given as the endorsers' statement. The fire and the 'not at the light' inference was reworded to 'does not link it to the light'. Close paraphrases of LighthouseFriends (entrance, lantern, pay and cow shed, skiff) were rewritten. OCR matched by position: the 1904 index line 'Currie, Archibald   Tobermory' sits on one OCR line inside the name-and-station block (between Casgrain and Cowan). The 1906 and 1907 indexes give the same pairing, and a 1909 salary table (OCR 'Tombermory Archibald Currie Oct. 12, 1903 ... 2.50', fuzzy) agrees on the 1903 appointment at $250. The page image itself could not be opened with the tools available, so the scan p.221 should still be looked at before publication. The Kingston News item and the 1885 departmental description are as LighthouseFriends quotes them; no original was read.
